7.	X is a young boy when his father performs a great sacrifice called the vishvajit yAga, which requires him to give away all his possessions. But the father gives away only old, barren cows that can no longer eat, drink, or give milk. Troubled by this hypocrisy, X asks his father: "To whom will you give me?" Annoyed, the father blurts out: "I give you to yama, the god of death." Obedient and resolute, X travels to yama's abode, but he is out of office. The boy waits at the doorstep for three days and nights without food or water. When yama returns, he is ashamed that a brAhmaNa guest has waited so long, and offers boons. X asks the ultimate question: what happens after death? Yama reveals the nature of the Atman (“soul”), using the famous metaphor of the body as a chariot, the intellect as the charioteer, the mind as the reins, and the senses as the horses. The name of the upanishad is often mistaken; the second consonant in the original name is hard, but it is a common mistake to assume that it is a soft consonant because the word then means story. W. Somerset Maugham used a quote from this Upanishad as the epigraph and title of his 1944 novel Z about an American's spiritual journey. ID X (10 points), Y (10 points), and Z (5 points).
Hint for Z: the epigraph, taken from this upanishad, is: “The sharp ____ of a _____ is difficult to pass over; thus the wise say the path to Salvation is hard.”
